The Wild Population Behind the Pet
text:
What Is a Wild Type Axolotl?
 A wild type axolotl is the natural color form of Ambystoma mexicanum, carrying the dominant D allele at the white locus and all three pigment cell types . It looks dark brown or olive-green with black, yellow, and iridescent speckles across the body and gills.
 Wild type is the baseline phenotype every other morph mutates from. Leucistic, golden albino, and melanoid axolotls carry recessive mutations at one or more pigment genes; a wild type carries none of those mutations as a homozygous pair.
 A wild type axolotl costs $25 to $60 , which makes it the most common and the least expensive morph sold by breeders.
 What Color Is a Wild Type Axolotl?
 A wild type axolotl is dark brown to olive-green, with black mottling, yellow patches, and a shiny gold ring around each pupil . Individual shade ranges from almost-black specimens to lighter tan animals, because pigment density varies between lines.
 Three pigment cell types create the pattern. Melanophores produce the dark brown and black pigment, xanthophores add the yellow and olive tones, and iridophores produce the metallic speckle effect across the body and gills.
 Yellow is strongest in juveniles and fades as the animal matures, while iridophores multiply as the axolotl approaches sexual maturity.
 How Does a Wild Type Compare to Other Morphs?
 The wild type is the only common morph that shows all three pigment cell types, because every other morph deletes or reduces at least one of them . Leucistic stops pigment-cell migration, golden albino removes melanophores, and melanoid removes iridophores.
 Here is how the four core morphs compare across the three pigment cell types:
 Morph Genotype Melanophores Xanthophores Iridophores 
 Wild type D/- A/- M/- Ax/- Present Present Present 
 Leucistic d/d Confined to eyes and crest Present Present 
 Golden albino D/- a/a Absent Present Present 
 Melanoid m/m Increased Reduced Absent 
 What Is the Wild Type Axolotl Genotype?
 The wild type axolotl genotype is D/- A/- M/- Ax/-, which means it is not homozygous for any of the four color mutations . The relevant genes are A (albino), M (melanoid), Ax (axanthic), and D (white locus).
 The D allele drives the production of yellow xanthophores, which combine with melanophores to create the wild type's brown-olive base color. A dash stands for the second allele, which is either dominant or recessive without changing the phenotype.
 A plain wild type cross produces 100% wild type offspring when neither parent carries a recessive color gene . Two wild types that both carry one albino allele (a) produce about 25% albino offspring.
 How Do You Tell a Wild Type from a Melanoid?
 The single reliable difference is the eye: a wild type has a shiny iridescent ring around the pupil, and a melanoid does not . Both animals appear dark brown or black at a glance.
 The melanoid mutation (m/m) reduces xanthophores, removes iridophores entirely, and multiplies melanophores. The result is a uniformly dark animal with no metallic shine anywhere on the body, including the eyes.
 A wild type shows the reflective eye ring even when its body is very dark. If no metallic ring surrounds the pupil under good light, the animal is a melanoid.
 A wild type also keeps visible yellow speckling and a brown undertone, where a melanoid reads as flat black or dark gray.
 Are Wild Type Axolotls Good Pets?
 Yes, a wild type axolotl requires exactly the same care as every other morph, because color genetics do not affect health, temperament, or husbandry . Tank size, temperature, water quality, and diet are identical across all morphs.
 Wild types are hardy and widely available from breeders, which makes them a sensible first axolotl. They eat the standard carnivore diet of earthworms, pellets, and frozen foods.
 The only real difference is visual. A keeper who wants the classic natural look chooses wild type; a keeper who wants the darkest animal buys a melanoid instead.
 If you already own a dark axolotl and are unsure which morph it is, the color genetics guide explains the genotype behind every morph .
 Browse all axolotl morphs and their colors to compare wild type against leucistic, golden albino, and the other forms.
 How Does a Wild Type Change with Age?
 A wild type's yellow tones fade and its iridescence strengthens as it matures, while the brown-olive base color stays constant . Juveniles show the yellow xanthophores most strongly, and adults show more metallic speckle across the body and gills.
 The silhouette, gill size, and eye ring do not change with age. Only the balance of yellow versus shine shifts between the juvenile and adult stages.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Yes, the wild type is the most common morph, because the phenotype needs no recessive mutation to express. Every other common morph requires a homozygous recessive pair to appear.
 Two wild types produce a melanoid only when both parents carry the recessive m allele. Otherwise the entire clutch is wild type.
 A wild type carrying one albino allele (A/a) looks fully wild type, because the dominant A masks the recessive a. It still passes the hidden allele to half of its offspring.
 Yes, the wild type is the standard natural form, and every other morph is a mutation of it. The term wild type means the unmutated baseline phenotype.
 Wild Type Variants and Color Intensity
 "Wild type" is a range, not a single shade. Wild-type axolotls carry all three pigment-cell types — melanophores, xanthophores, and iridophores — and the balance of those cells decides whether an individual reads dark black-brown, olive, or a brighter "high-yellow" animal. This is the same three-cell mechanism covered in the pigment-cells guide , and it means no two wild types are exactly the same colour.
 Rarity, Price, and Availability
 The wild type is the baseline and one of the cheapest morphs to buy, usually from around $25. Because they are the natural form, they are widely available from reputable breeders and pet stores. Prices sit on the price-by-morph page ; for buyer advice see breeder vs pet store .
 The Wild Population Behind the Pet
 Wild-type is the colour of the wild axolotl — but the wild population is critically endangered and survives only in the canals of Xochimilco near Mexico City. Pet wild types are captive-bred, never taken from the wild. For the animal's true situation, see the Xochimilco habitat and conservation status .

title: Chimera Axolotl: The Rarest Morph of All
dek: A chimera axolotl is a single animal built from two fused embryos, so it carries two complete sets of DNA and shows two different color patterns. The body splits cleanly down th...
headings: What Is a Chimera Axolotl?
How Rare Is a Chimera Axolotl?
How Much Does a Chimera Axolotl Cost?
Is a Chimera a Real Morph?
Are Chimeras and Mosaics the Same?
Can You Breed Chimera Axolotls?
What Is a Firefly Axolotl?
Frequently Asked Questions
text:
What Is a Chimera Axolotl?
 A chimera axolotl is a single animal built from two fused embryos, so it carries two complete sets of DNA and shows two different color patterns . The body splits cleanly down the midline in most chimeras, with one side the color of the first embryo and the other side the color of the second.
 This condition is called chimerism, and it is a developmental accident, not a trait passed through genes. A chimera is half wild type and half leucistic, or any other pairing of two standard morph colors, because each half belongs to a different original embryo.
 The split is visible because the two cell lines develop side by side from the earliest cell divisions, and each line keeps producing its own pigment cells.
 How Rare Is a Chimera Axolotl?
 A chimera axolotl survives to adulthood in 1 in 10 million cases, which makes it the rarest phenotype in the hobby by a wide margin . Most chimeras never reach that point.
 Two factors make survival this unlikely. The fusion itself is rare, and most fused embryos die during development or hatch with severe defects.
 Most chimeras that hatch do not reach maturity. The two genomes produce incompatible organ development, and many die in their first year from incomplete heart or digestive connections.
 How Much Does a Chimera Axolotl Cost?
 An adult chimera axolotl sells for $300 to over $1,000 when one is offered at all . Living adult chimeras are almost never listed for sale, because so few survive to that stage.
 The price reflects rarity, not genetics. A chimera carries no unique gene, so its value comes only from the one-in-ten-million split appearance.
 Is a Chimera a Real Morph?
 No, a chimera is not a morph, because it is a developmental accident that cannot be bred for or predicted . Morphs like leucistic, golden albino, and melanoid are heritable and appear in predictable ratios; a chimera appears only by chance when two embryos fuse.
 Because the trait is not genetic, a chimera cannot pass its split pattern to offspring. Breeding a chimera produces normal offspring in the normal ratios for its component morphs, with no increased chance of another chimera.
 Some sellers list chimeras alongside morphs for convenience, but biologically the two categories differ. A morph is one genotype; a chimera is two genotypes in one animal.
 Are Chimeras and Mosaics the Same?
 No, a chimera and a mosaic axolotl are different conditions, even though they look similar . A chimera comes from two embryos fusing; a mosaic comes from a single embryo that carries a genetic change in only some of its cells.
 A mosaic has one set of DNA with a mutation that appears in only part of the body, while a chimera has two complete, separate genomes. The visible result looks similar, but the cause differs.
 In practice, keepers use the terms interchangeably, because both produce patchy, two-tone animals. For a breeding decision the distinction matters: neither can be selected for.
 A chimera is occasionally called a split-mosaic because of the clean midline division.
 Can You Breed Chimera Axolotls?
 No, you cannot breed chimera axolotls, because the fusion that creates them cannot be forced . Attempted artificial fusion of embryos fails or kills the eggs.
 Most chimeras are also sterile, and many have internal organ connections that never form completely. Ethical breeders treat a living chimera as a display animal, not a breeding animal.
 Because of the health risks and the rarity, most adult chimeras live in research facilities or with breeders who specialize in rare genetics.
 If you want to understand the genetic ratios behind normal, breedable morphs, the Punnett square guide works through real crosses .
 What Is a Firefly Axolotl?
 A firefly axolotl is a chimera-type animal made by experimental embryonic grafting, in which one embryo's GFP tail is attached to another embryo's body . The tail glows neon green under UV light, and the body shows the second embryo's color.
 Researchers and specialized breeders produce fireflies by grafting tissue before the embryo finishes developing. The result is a deliberate chimera, unlike the accidental fusions that create naturally occurring split-color chimeras.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 A chimera axolotl is two different colors because it began as two separate embryos that fused, so each half of the body carries the pigment genes of a different embryo.
 Most chimera axolotls are not healthy; mortality is high, many are sterile, and some have incomplete internal organ connections. Survivors need normal axolotl care plus close observation.
 An adult chimera sells for $300 to $1,000 or more when one is offered at all. Most chimeras never reach saleable size.
 No, you cannot get a chimera from breeding your axolotls, because chimerism is a chance fusion event that no pair of parents can produce on demand.
 Explore the full list of axolotl morphs to see which colors are actually breedable.

title: Axolotl Egg and Larvae Care: A Complete Guide
dek: Axolotl eggs hatch in about 15 days at 20°C (68°F), in under 14 days at 25°C (77°F), and in more than 20 days at 18°C (64°F). Temperature is the sole control over hatching speed.
headings: How Long Do Axolotl Eggs Take to Hatch?
How Many Eggs Does an Axolotl Lay?
How Do You Set Up a Tank for Axolotl Eggs?
Do Axolotl Eggs Need Special Water?
How Do You Prevent Fungus on Axolotl Eggs?
What Do You Do When Axolotl Eggs Hatch?
How Do You Feed and Raise Axolotl Larvae?
Frequently Asked Questions
text:
How Long Do Axolotl Eggs Take to Hatch?
 Axolotl eggs hatch in about 15 days at 20°C (68°F), in under 14 days at 25°C (77°F), and in more than 20 days at 18°C (64°F) . Temperature is the sole control over hatching speed.
 Keeping eggs warmer accelerates development but shrinks the window to prepare food. Keeping them cooler buys an extra week or two to set up live food cultures.
 A female lays 100 to 1,500 eggs in a single clutch, deposited individually on plants, decor, or the tank glass. Each egg sits inside a protective jelly layer.
 How Many Eggs Does an Axolotl Lay?
 A female axolotl lays 100 to 1,500 eggs in a single clutch , placed one at a time over one to two days. Her size and age determine the exact number.
 Eggs are laid individually rather than in a mass, each attached to a surface by a jelly layer. Live plants are the preferred egg site when they are available.
 How Do You Set Up a Tank for Axolotl Eggs?
 Move the eggs to a separate hatching tank filled with dechlorinated water before they hatch . A small tank around 45 x 20 x 25 cm (18 x 8 x 10 in) is enough for a clutch of about 100 eggs.
 Axolotl eggs are tough. Remove them by slicing the jelly attachment point with a fingernail, or move the plants the eggs are stuck to.
 Keep the water temperature near 20°C (68°F) for a steady 14-to-16-day hatch, and use water that is not soft, because dissolved salts support normal embryo development.
 Do Axolotl Eggs Need Special Water?
 No, axolotl eggs need the same dechlorinated water as adult axolotls, with ammonia and nitrite at 0 ppm and a pH between 7 and 8.4 . No medication or special salt mix is required for normal hatching.
 Use water from a cycled, mature tank when possible, because it contains the beneficial bacteria that keep ammonia at zero. Do not put eggs into freshly filled, uncycled water.
 Partial water changes of about 10% every few days keep the water clean without disturbing the eggs.
 How Do You Prevent Fungus on Axolotl Eggs?
 White, cloudy eggs are unfertilized or dead, and removing them is the main defense against fungus spreading to viable eggs . A gentle water flow over the clutch also prevents fungal growth.
 Fertile eggs darken as the embryo develops, so a pearly, translucent egg that stays clear is the one to watch. Check the clutch daily and lift out every opaque white egg the day it appears.
 What Do You Do When Axolotl Eggs Hatch?
 Keep the larvae undisturbed for the first 24 to 72 hours after hatching, because they live on their yolk sac and need no food . Newly hatched larvae measure 10 to 13 mm (about half an inch) and stay motionless during this period.
 Start feeding live baby brine shrimp as the first food once the yolk is absorbed , because larvae this small eat only live food that moves.
 Lower the water level to about 3 to 4 cm before hatching so that food concentrates near the larvae and they reach it easily.
 Tear the jelly coat of eggs that have not hatched once the rest of the clutch is out, because a larva left sealed inside the jelly suffocates.
 How Do You Feed and Raise Axolotl Larvae?
 Feed larvae once or twice daily and keep a maximum of 25 larvae per 45 x 20 x 25 cm tank . Overcrowding starves the slowest larvae and fouls the water.
 The first foods in order of preference are newly hatched brine shrimp, small daphnia, and microworms . Brine shrimp and daphnia are the most nutritious; microworms alone produce slow growth.
 At 20°C, larvae reach about 1.5 cm within the first week . Front legs develop at roughly 20 mm, which takes about 9 days at 22°C, and hind legs follow at the end of the third week.
 When larvae reach about 2.5 to 4 cm, they begin taking finely chopped bloodworm or small axolotl pellets. Separate them by size to stop larger larvae from biting smaller ones.
 Cull any larvae with obvious deformities, because poorly formed animals rarely recover and they waste resources needed to grow healthy siblings.
 Once your larvae are past the egg stage, the juvenile raising guide covers feeding, growth, and rehoming .
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Yes, you can move axolotl eggs without hurting them, because the jelly layer protects the embryo and the egg is tough. Slice the attachment point and lift the egg clear.
 Yes, adult axolotls eat their own eggs and larvae, so remove the adults or the eggs as soon as laying finishes.
 White, cloudy eggs are unfertilized or dead; remove them to prevent fungus spreading to healthy eggs.
 25°C (77°F) hatches eggs fastest, in under 14 days, but the fastest hatch leaves the least time to prepare live food.
 See the full axolotl breeding guide for conditioning, courtship, and egg laying.

title: Axolotl Genetics and Inbreeding Risk
dek: Most captive axolotls descend from a tiny founder population of 34 animals imported to Paris in 1863, and research colonies carry an inbreeding coefficient near 35%. That coeffi...
headings: Why Are Axolotls So Inbred?
What Does Inbreeding Do to Axolotls?
When Is Breeding Two Axolotls Unsafe?
How Do You Breed Axolotls Ethically?
How Many Times Can a Female Axolotl Breed?
Frequently Asked Questions
text:
Why Are Axolotls So Inbred?
 Most captive axolotls descend from a tiny founder population of 34 animals imported to Paris in 1863, and research colonies carry an inbreeding coefficient near 35% . That coefficient sits far above the 12% level that marks first-cousin breeding.
 Captive axolotls have less genetic variety than wild populations, because every generation in a closed colony reshuffles a shrinking pool of genes. Even axolotls from different breeders share recent ancestors, since breeders routinely trade and purchase from one another.
 The wild population is critically endangered and nearly gone from its native canals, so adding new wild genes is not a practical option for most hobbyists.
 What Does Inbreeding Do to Axolotls?
 Inbreeding makes offspring homozygous for harmful recessive genes, which produces deformities, reduced fertility, weaker immune systems, and higher death rates . This cluster of effects is called inbreeding depression.
 There are 5 common signs of inbred lines: dwarfism, short toes, gill abnormalities, poor limb regeneration, and a tendency toward recurring illness or fungus.
 Fertility also drops in inbred lines. Breeders who have kept closed colonies for decades report smaller clutches, more unfertilized eggs, and more deformed larvae than in fresh lines.
 In a single clutch, deformity rate is the practical test. A healthy pair produces mostly normal larvae, while a badly inbred pair throws visible defects in a meaningful share of offspring.
 When Is Breeding Two Axolotls Unsafe?
 Breeding is unsafe whenever two axolotls share an ancestor within three generations, or when either animal carries a known genetic defect . Sibling, parent-to-offspring, and cousin crosses all concentrate recessive mutations.
 Do not breed animals with a physical deformation that is not a healed bite, animals that float upside down repeatedly, or animals with chronic health problems such as frequent fungus.
 If a male and female have been kept together and eggs appear, and the pair has any chance of being related, cull the eggs rather than raise hundreds of potentially defective animals.
 Freeze eggs from an unknown or possibly inbred pair to dispose of them, because releasing or keeping them spreads the defective genes.
 How Do You Breed Axolotls Ethically?
 Ethical breeding pairs fully grown, healthy, unrelated stock and raises a maximum of 10 eggs from a first clutch . A first-time breeder starts with a small number rather than a full clutch.
 Breed only females at least a year old, fully grown, with a round belly and a strong appetite. Select males whose family history you know.
 Trade animals with other breeders to add genetic variety to your lines. Avoid buying a breeding pair or a whole breeding group from a single source unless you know the group has a large, varied gene pool.
 If you need the offspring to have a specific color, the Punnett square guide predicts offspring ratios .
 How Many Times Can a Female Axolotl Breed?
 A female axolotl breeds a maximum of three times in her lifetime and never more than once per year , because egg production is an exhausting energy cost.
 Each breeding cycle drains her mineral stores and condition. Spacing clutches by at least 12 months lets her regain weight between seasons.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Most captive axolotls are inbred, because the global population descends from a small number of founders; the inbreeding coefficient in research colonies is about 35%.
 No, do not breed siblings even when they look healthy, because sibling crosses concentrate recessive defects and raise the offspring's risk of deformity and disease.
 You cannot tell whether eggs are inbred by looking at them; confirm the parents' family history before breeding, or treat the clutch as potentially inbred.
 Freeze unwanted eggs to dispose of them humanely, and never release eggs or axolotls into the wild.
 Start with the axolotl breeding guide for the full breeding process.

title: Breeding Triggers: Temperature Cycling for Axolotls
dek: You trigger axolotl breeding by cooling the water over about 2 weeks, holding it at 12 to 14°C for 4 to 6 weeks, then warming it back to 20 to 22°C. This temperature cycle is th...
headings: How Do You Trigger Axolotl Breeding?
What Temperature Triggers Axolotl Breeding?
What Happens During Axolotl Courtship?
How Many Eggs Will an Axolotl Lay?
When Is the Axolotl Breeding Season?
How Do You Know When Axolotls Are Ready to Breed?
Frequently Asked Questions
text:
How Do You Trigger Axolotl Breeding?
 You trigger axolotl breeding by cooling the water over about 2 weeks, holding it at 12 to 14°C for 4 to 6 weeks, then warming it back to 20 to 22°C . This temperature cycle is the most reliable way to induce spawning in captivity.
 Two trigger methods work in practice. The first is a gradual temperature cycle that mimics winter into spring. The second is a thermal shock, where a male kept at 20 to 22°C is moved into water at least 5°C colder, around 12 to 14°C, which triggers courtship within days in most pairs.
 Day length also matters. Shorten the light period for a few weeks, then lengthen it steadily, the pattern of winter into spring, to drive breeding behavior in most pairs.
 Keep the conditioning pair well fed with protein-rich foods such as earthworms throughout the cooling period, because breeding requires significant energy.
 What Temperature Triggers Axolotl Breeding?
 Condition breeders at 20 to 22°C (68 to 71°F) for 4 to 6 weeks, then drop the water to 12 to 14°C (54 to 57°F) . A temperature drop of at least 5°C is required to trigger courtship behavior.
 Keep the pair at the cool temperature for the full conditioning period, then raise it gradually back toward normal range. The warming phase is what prompts egg laying.
 Temperatures above 24°C stress axolotls and cause failed clutches, so keep the breeding tank below this limit at all times.
 A chiller gives precise control over the cycle. A cool room or partial cold water changes are the low-cost alternatives.
 Here is the full breeding cycle at a glance:
 Stage Temperature Duration Key action 
 Conditioning 20-22°C (68-71°F) 4-6 weeks Feed protein-rich food, shorten daylight 
 Cool-down Drop to 12-14°C (54-57°F) About 2 weeks Lower the water gradually 
 Cold hold 12-14°C (54-57°F) 4-6 weeks Keep the pair well fed 
 Warm-up Back to 20-22°C (68-71°F) 1-2 weeks Lengthen daylight steadily 
 Courtship 12-14°C, then rising 1-3 days Male deposits spermatophores 
 Egg laying 20-22°C (68-71°F) 12-72 hours after fertilization Female lays eggs individually 
 What Happens During Axolotl Courtship?
 Courtship ends with the male depositing spermatophores, small packets of sperm, on the substrate and the female drawing them into her cloaca . The male initiates by nudging the female and performing a display dance.
 The male leads the female and deposits a line of spermatophores, then blocks her path so she brushes over them. She picks up the sperm with her cloaca, which sits just behind her back legs.
 This stage lasts one to three days. The female then lays eggs 12 to 72 hours after fertilization , individually, on plants, decor, or the glass.
 How Many Eggs Will an Axolotl Lay?
 A female axolotl lays up to 1,500 eggs in a single clutch , deposited one at a time over a day or two. The exact number depends on her size and age.
 Eggs are laid individually rather than in a mass, each attached to a surface by a jelly layer. Plants are the preferred egg site if they are available.
 Remove the adults as soon as laying finishes, because adult axolotls eat their own eggs and larvae.
 If you plan to raise the clutch, move the eggs or the plants into a separate hatching tank and follow the egg and larvae care guide .
 When Is the Axolotl Breeding Season?
 The natural axolotl breeding season runs from December to June, with peak activity in late winter and early spring . In the wild, this is when the water sits at 12 to 14°C with roughly 11 hours of daylight.
 Captive breeding simulates the same signal, so axolotls breed at any time of year with the right temperature and light cycling.
 How Do You Know When Axolotls Are Ready to Breed?
 A ready female looks oval from above, and a mature male shows an enlarged cloaca . Both animals are at least 18 months old before pairing.
 Sex your animals with the sexing guide before pairing them. If a pair does not breed, confirm the male and female are 18 months or older, well fed, and conditioned through a full cool period before trying again.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Yes, axolotls can breed at any time of year when temperature and light cycling mimic the seasons.
 Axolotl eggs hatch in about 15 days at 20°C (68°F) , in under 14 days at 25°C (77°F), and in more than 20 days at 18°C (64°F).
 Yes, adult axolotls eat their own eggs, so remove the adults or the eggs as soon as laying finishes.
 If your pair does not breed, confirm both animals are a confirmed male and female at least 18 months old, well fed, and conditioned through a full cool period.
 See the complete axolotl breeding guide for the full process.

title: How to Tell Axolotl Gender (Sexing Guide)
dek: An axolotl is reliably sexable at 18 months, because until that age every juvenile looks female. Before 18 months, every axolotl shows only a small, downward-pointing cloaca.
headings: When Can You Tell an Axolotl's Gender?
How Do You Tell a Male Axolotl?
How Do You Tell a Female Axolotl?
Do Male and Female Axolotls Look Different?
Can a Female Cloaca Look Like a Male's?
Are There Early Signs of Gender in Juveniles?
Frequently Asked Questions
text:
When Can You Tell an Axolotl's Gender?
 An axolotl is reliably sexable at 18 months, because until that age every juvenile looks female . Before 18 months, every axolotl shows only a small, downward-pointing cloaca.
 Males develop an enlarged cloaca between 8 and 12 months old , though some late bloomers show it only at 18 months. Until 18 months, you cannot rule out male or female with certainty.
 Do not trust a pet store's sexing of a young juvenile. Young axolotls are sold labeled male or female before the characteristics exist.
 How Do You Tell a Male Axolotl?
 A male axolotl has an enlarged cloaca that bulges outward from the sides of its body . This is the single reliable indicator of a male.
 The bulge appears as a wider, swollen area just behind the back legs, best viewed from directly behind the axolotl or from above.
 Males are also slimmer with a longer tail than females in most pairs, but body shape varies enough that it is never the deciding factor.
 A mature male also develops small breeding tubercles on its head, tail, and limbs during the breeding season, which females do not grow.
 How Do You Tell a Female Axolotl?
 A female axolotl has a small cloaca that protrudes only downward, with no side bulge . Every axolotl, including every young male, shows this shape until the male's cloaca enlarges.
 Females are plumper and rounder with a shorter tail than males. A gravid female carrying eggs is visibly swollen in the abdomen, and in some cases eggs are visible through her skin.
 Because the female cloaca looks exactly like an immature male's cloaca, you cannot conclude female until the animal is 18 months old and the cloaca has clearly stayed small.
 Do Male and Female Axolotls Look Different?
 Beyond the cloaca, male and female axolotls look nearly identical, and the differences that exist are averages, not rules . Color, gill size, and head shape do not tell you the sex.
 On average, males are slimmer with longer tails and slightly larger heads, while females are rounder and, in most pairs, larger overall. None of these is decisive on its own.
 The only decisive difference is the cloaca: enlarged and side-bulging in a mature male, small and downward in a female.
 Can a Female Cloaca Look Like a Male's?
 Yes, a female's cloaca swells temporarily before a bowel movement, which produces a false male reading . The bulge disappears once she defecates.
 Check the cloaca again a few hours later. If the rounded bulge persists after the animal has passed waste, it is a mature male.
 Are There Early Signs of Gender in Juveniles?
 One early female indicator is the oviducts visible through the translucent skin of young juveniles, but it is not definitive . Oviducts are female-specific organs that keepers mistake for intestines.
 Transparency fades as juveniles grow, so this clue is only usable in the first months. Treat 18 months as the only reliable deadline for a confident answer.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 No, an axolotl's sex is fixed at birth and never changes during its life.
 A cloaca with no side bulge reads as female or too young to tell, so do not definitively sex a juvenile.
 Size is not the test; age is, so wait until at least 18 months, then check the cloaca.
 No, you do not need two axolotls to determine gender, because the cloaca test works on a single animal at any time.
 Once you know you have a confirmed pair, the breeding triggers guide explains how to start .
 Explore the full axolotl breeding section for the complete process.

title: Raising Baby Axolotls (Juveniles) to Adulthood
dek: Newly hatched axolotl larvae eat only live baby brine shrimp for their first weeks, because they respond to movement, not smell. They ignore dead food until they are much larger.
headings: What Do Newly Hatched Axolotls Eat?
How Often Do You Feed Baby Axolotls?
When Do Baby Axolotls Develop Legs?
Why Are Baby Axolotls Biting Each Other?
How Do You Cull Deformed Axolotl Larvae?
When Do You Rehome Baby Axolotls?
Frequently Asked Questions
text:
What Do Newly Hatched Axolotls Eat?
 Newly hatched axolotl larvae eat only live baby brine shrimp for their first weeks, because they respond to movement, not smell . They ignore dead food until they are much larger.
 Larvae survive on their yolk sac for the first 24 to 72 hours, then must eat. The first live food options are newly hatched brine shrimp, small daphnia, or moina, in that order of preference.
 Hatch your own brine shrimp rather than buying it, because store-bought shrimp are too old, too large, and nutritionally spent. Freshly hatched shrimp carry an egg sac that makes them far more nutritious.
 Remove unhatched brine shrimp eggs and shells before feeding, because the hard shells can block a larva's intestines.
 How Often Do You Feed Baby Axolotls?
 Feed baby axolotls once or twice a day while they are on live food, then twice daily as juveniles . Growing axolotls need daily feeding to develop properly, unlike adults that eat every two to three days.
 Larvae at 20°C grow to about 1.5 cm within the first week with daily feeding. At 22°C, front legs begin at roughly 20 mm, around day 9, and hind legs appear at the end of the third week.
 Partial water changes daily are required when feeding brine shrimp, because the shrimp die quickly in fresh water and foul it within hours. Daphnia, by contrast, live in the tank until eaten and need less frequent changes.
 When Do Baby Axolotls Develop Legs?
 Front legs start as buds at about 20 mm, which takes roughly 9 days at 22°C, and hind legs follow at the end of the third week . The timeline depends directly on temperature and feeding frequency.
 The lungs develop around the same time as the hind legs, even though axolotls keep their external gills for life.
 When the front legs finish developing and the hind legs are visible, the larvae become miniature versions of adults and are then called juveniles.
 Once juveniles reach about 2.5 to 4 cm, they begin taking finely chopped bloodworm, small axolotl pellets, or small pieces of earthworm . Introduce each new food gradually, because it takes several days for juveniles to recognize a new food as edible.
 Why Are Baby Axolotls Biting Each Other?
 Baby axolotls become cannibalistic as soon as their front legs develop, biting the gills and limbs of smaller siblings . Size segregation is the only reliable prevention.
 Keep larvae of similar size together, and move any animal that grows noticeably faster into its own container immediately. Bites cost the victim energy meant for growth, and a badly bitten larva dies.
 Most breeders move each juvenile into its own container as soon as it has front feet, which eliminates bites entirely at the cost of more tubs.
 Keep density low in shared tanks. At 25 mm, hold a maximum of 25 larvae per 45 x 20 x 25 cm tank, and thin them out as they grow.
 How Do You Cull Deformed Axolotl Larvae?
 Cull any larva with a visible deformity or an inability to regrow limbs by freezing it, because these animals rarely recover and they waste resources on a defective line . Axolotls have a long history of inbreeding, so defects are more common than in most species.
 The humane method is freezing: place the larvae in a small container and freeze them, which puts them into a hibernation state and dulls their sense of pain before vital functions stop.
 Culling is standard practice among ethical breeders and is preferable to raising deformed animals that would carry the defects into the gene pool.
 When Do You Rehome Baby Axolotls?
 Start finding homes for juveniles when they reach about 5 cm, before they outgrow their grow-out tanks . Do not release them into the wild, and never sell them without disclosing the parents' genetics.
 By 8 to 9 cm, move juveniles into larger containers with more water, because they need roughly the same space and water quality as a small adult tank.
 Disclose the parents' morphs and any known genetics to buyers, especially if there is any chance the parents were related.
 If the parents were possibly inbred, find a breeder or herpetological society to take the clutch instead of raising it yourself.
 You started this journey at hatching, so the egg and larvae care guide covers the stage before this one.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Newly hatched larvae require food within 24 to 72 hours of hatching, once their yolk sac is gone.
 Frozen bloodworm works as a juvenile food once the larvae reach 2.5 to 4 cm with front legs, which takes about 8 to 10 weeks.
 With daily feeding at 20°C, larvae reach about 1.5 cm in the first week and about 7 cm by 3 months.
 Baby axolotls need a gentle air stone plus daily water changes, not a strong filter, because young larvae cannot handle current.
 See the full axolotl breeding guide for the complete process from conditioning to rehoming.

title: Axolotl Color Genetics: Punnett Squares Explained
dek: Axolotl color is controlled by four recessive pigment genes, a (albino), m (melanoid), ax (axanthic), and d (white), inherited independently across 14 pairs of chromosomes. An a...
headings: How Do Axolotl Color Genes Work?
How Do You Read an Axolotl Punnett Square?
What Does a Melanoid Cross Produce?
What Does an Albino Cross Produce?
How Do You Combine Two Genes?
What Genotype Produces Each Morph?
Frequently Asked Questions
Limitations of Punnett Squares
Worked Example: Leucistic x Albino (Two-Gene Cross)
text:
How Do Axolotl Color Genes Work?
 Axolotl color is controlled by four recessive pigment genes, a (albino), m (melanoid), ax (axanthic), and d (white), inherited independently across 14 pairs of chromosomes . An axolotl has 28 chromosomes in 14 pairs, and the color genes sit on pairs without linkage to each other.
 Each gene has two alleles, one from each parent. A dominant allele, written with a capital letter, masks a recessive allele, written lowercase. An animal must carry two copies of a recessive allele, such as m/m, to show that morph.
 Three pigment cell types create color. Melanophores produce black-brown pigment, xanthophores produce yellow, and iridophores produce metallic shine. Each pigment gene reduces or removes one or more of these cell types.
 The wild type phenotype requires no recessive allele and shows all three pigment cells.
 How Do You Read an Axolotl Punnett Square?
 A Punnett square places one parent's two alleles along the top and the other parent's two alleles down the side, then combines each pair to show every possible offspring genotype . Each of the four boxes represents one possible genotype at 25% odds.
 Build the square for a single gene at a time. For the melanoid gene, a melanoid parent contributes m and m, and a wild type carrier contributes M and m.
 The genotype written in each box is the combination of one allele from each parent, and the phenotype shown depends on whether the recessive allele is present twice.
 The percentages in the four boxes are per-offspring odds, not a guarantee across a clutch.
 What Does a Melanoid Cross Produce?
 Crossing a melanoid (m/m) with a wild type carrier (M/m) produces 50% melanoid and 50% wild type offspring . Each offspring has a 1 in 2 chance of receiving m from both parents.
 Here is the Punnett square for m/m x M/m:
 M m 
 m M/m m/m 
 m M/m m/m 
 Two wild type carriers (M/m x M/m) produce 25% melanoid, 50% wild type carriers, and 25% wild type with no m allele . Two melanoids (m/m x m/m) produce 100% melanoid.
 An axolotl is a melanoid only with the genotype m/m. A single M allele produces a normal wild type appearance.
 What Does an Albino Cross Produce?
 Crossing an albino (a/a) with a wild type carrier (A/a) produces 50% albino and 50% wild type that carry the albino gene . The a allele is recessive, so two a's are required to remove melanin.
 Here is the Punnett square for a/a x A/a:
 A a 
 a A/a a/a 
 a A/a a/a 
 Two albinos (a/a x a/a) produce 100% albino offspring, while two wild type carriers (A/a x A/a) produce 25% albino.
 Albinos lack eumelanin, so they appear white or golden with pink or red eyes and gills, depending on which other genes they carry.
 How Do You Combine Two Genes?
 To predict the color of offspring that differ in two genes, build a 16-box Punnett square using all four allele combinations from each parent . Each of the 16 boxes is one possible genotype at 6.25% odds.
 For example, a golden albino (a/a D/+) bred with a leucistic (d/d A/+) needs a cross for both the albino and the white gene. First determine each parent's four possible allele pairs: a/a gives only a, while D/+ gives D or +.
 Combine them into a 4 x 4 grid the same way you combine a 2 x 2. Add the boxes with the same phenotype to find the percentage of each color in the clutch.
 The white gene (d/d) changes pigment distribution rather than pigment production, which is why d/d with A/+ gives a leucistic and d/d with a/a gives a white albino.
 What Genotype Produces Each Morph?
 Wild type is D/-, leucistic is d/d, golden albino is a/a with D/-, and melanoid is m/m . Each morph is defined by one homozygous recessive pair plus the dominant alleles at every other locus.
 Here is how the core morphs map to genotypes and pigment changes:
 Morph Genotype Pigment change 
 Wild type D/- A/- M/- Ax/- All three pigment cells present 
 Leucistic d/d Pigment cells fail to migrate from the neural crest 
 Golden albino a/a with D/- Melanophores absent, xanthophores kept 
 Melanoid m/m Iridophores absent, melanophores increased 
 White albino d/d a/a No pigment migration plus no melanophores 
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Axolotls have four main pigment genes, a (albino), m (melanoid), ax (axanthic), and d (white), plus newer mutations still being studied.
 A melanoid has no shiny eye ring because the m/m genotype removes iridophores entirely, so the metallic ring around the pupil that other morphs show is absent.
 Two wild types produce a leucistic only when both carry the d allele, with 25% odds for a d/d x d/d carrier cross.
 A golden albino is a/a with a functional D allele, so it lacks melanophores but keeps the yellow xanthophores.
 A wild type genotype is D/- A/- M/- Ax/-, meaning it carries no homozygous recessive color pair.
 Start with the axolotl morphs hub to see each color, and check the breeding guide for how genetics fit into breeding decisions.
 Limitations of Punnett Squares
 Punnett squares predict outcomes at a single locus, which makes them the right tool for the classic diallelic genes (leucistic, albino, melanoid, axanthic). They cannot predict how an animal will look when genetics play out unpredictably: chimeras arise from fused embryos (two separate animals in one), mosaics from a mutation in one embryonic cell line, and GFP and copper intensity vary with polygenic modifiers rather than one gene. For those cases the biology is covered in the pigment-cells guide .
 Worked Example: Leucistic x Albino (Two-Gene Cross)
 Each gene resolves independently. For the white locus, a leucistic parent (d/d) bred to a wild-color carrier (D/d) gives 50% leucistic and 50% wild colour for that locus. The albino locus works the same way as a separate diallelic recessive. So a single pairing reads as two independent 50/50 flips: roughly a quarter of the clutch can end up showing the albino trait, a quarter leucistic, a quarter leucistic+albino (both recessives), and a quarter visibly wild type — before considering pigment intensity, which Punnett squares do not model.

title: Leucistic Axolotl: The "Lucy" Morph
dek: A leucistic axolotl is a pale pink to white axolotl with dark eyes and bright pink or red gills, produced by the recessive d/d genotype at the white locus. It is the most common...
headings: What Is a Leucistic Axolotl?
How Is a Leucistic Different from an Albino?
What Is a Dirty Lucy Axolotl?
How Do Leucistic Axolotl Crosses Come Out?
Do Leucistic Axolotls Need Different Care?
Frequently Asked Questions
How Rare Is a Leucistic Axolotl, and What Does One Cost?
